'''''Thief II: The Metal Age''''' is a 2000 [[stealth game|stealth]] video game developed by [[Looking Glass Studios]] and published by [[Eidos Interactive]] in March 2000. Like its predecessor ''[[Thief: The Dark Project]]'', the game follows [[Garrett (Thief)|Garrett]], a master thief who works in and around a [[steampunk]] metropolis called the City. The player assumes the role of Garrett as he unravels a conspiracy related to a new religious sect. Garrett takes on missions such as [[burglary|burglaries]] and [[frameup]]s, while trying to avoid detection by guards and automated security.

''Thief II'' was designed to build on the foundation of its predecessor. In response to feedback from players of ''Thief'', the team placed a heavy focus on urban stealth in the sequel, and they minimized the use of monsters and maze-like levels. The game was made with the third iteration of the [[Dark Engine]], which had been used previously to develop ''Thief'' and ''[[System Shock 2]]''. ''Thief II'' was announced at the 1999 [[Electronic Entertainment Expo]], as part of an extended contract between Looking Glass and Eidos to release games in the [[Thief (series)|''Thief'' series]]. Looking Glass neared bankruptcy as the game was developed, and the company was kept running by advances from Eidos.

''Thief II'' received positive reviews from critics, and its initial sales were stronger than those of its predecessor. However, the game's royalties were processed slowly, which compounded Looking Glass's financial troubles. As a result, the company closed in May 2000, with plans for ''Thief III'' cancelled. The third game in the series, entitled ''[[Thief: Deadly Shadows]]'', was developed by [[Ion Storm]] and published by Eidos in 2004. ''Thief 2X: Shadows of the Metal Age'', a widely praised expansion [[Mod (video gaming)|mod]] for ''Thief II'', was released in 2005. In 2014, [[Square Enix]] published a [[Thief (2014 video game)|reboot of the series]], developed by [[Eidos-Montréal]].

==Gameplay==
[[File:Thief 2 screenshot first city bank guard.jpg|left|thumb|The player holds the [[Baton (law enforcement)|blackjack]] and hides in a shadow from a patrolling guard. The light monitor in the bottom-center of the screen is completely dark, indicating that the player character is not visible to the enemy.]]
''Thief II'' is a [[stealth game]] that takes place from a [[first person (video games)|first-person perspective]] in a [[3D computer graphics|three-dimensional]] (3D) graphical environment.<ref name=cgwrev>{{cite magazine|last=L. McDonald |first=Thomas |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20010211210140/http://www.zdnet.com/cgw/stories/main/0%2C11529%2C2559422%2C00.html |url=http://www.zdnet.com/cgw/stories/main/0,11529,2559422,00.html |title=Stealing Beauty |magazine=[[Computer Gaming World]] |date=May 9, 2000 |archive-date=February 11, 2001 |url-status=dead }}</ref> The player seeks to complete mission objectives and to evade the notice of opponents such as guards.<ref name=cgmrev /><ref name=nytimes />  The player must minimize the visibility and audibility of the [[player character]], [[Garrett (Thief)|Garrett]], to escape detection. Players try to avoid lit areas and loud [[flooring]] in favor of shadows and quiet flooring. A light monitor on the [[HUD (video gaming)|heads-up display]] (HUD) indicates the player character's visibility.<ref name=manual>{{cite book | last=Hart | first=Dorian | year=2000 | title=Thief II: The Metal Age ''manual'' | publisher=Eidos Interactive | pages=5, 9, 11, 12, 17, 18, 20, 26, 27, 30, 34 }}</ref> While it is possible for the player character to engage in direct combat, he is easily defeated.<ref name=nytimes />

The game's 15 missions take place in large [[Level (video gaming)|levels]] that can be confronted in multiple ways.<ref name=cgwrev /><ref name=pczonerev>{{cite journal | last=Presley | first=Paul | title=''Thief II: The Metal Age'' | date=April 2000 | issue=88 | journal=[[PC Zone]] | pages=68–71 }}</ref> Guards may be knocked out with a [[Baton (law enforcement)|blackjack]] or killed with a bow or sword, and their fallen bodies may be picked up and hidden.<ref name=manual /> In addition to human enemies, the game features security [[automaton]]s and surveillance cameras.<ref name=pcgamerus /> While completing objectives such as [[frameup]]s and blackmail, the player steals valuables that may be used to purchase thieving gear between missions.<ref name=nytimes /><ref name=manual /><ref name=pczonerev /> The player's main tools are specialized arrows, including water arrows to douse lights, moss arrows to dampen the player character's footsteps and rope arrows to reach higher ground.<ref name=cgwrev />

''Thief II'' is designed to be played methodically,<ref name=cgwrev /> and the player plans ahead by scouting, reading the game's map and observing patrol patterns.<ref name=manual /> The player character has a [[Zoom lens|zooming]] mechanical eye, which connects to throwable "Scouting Orb" cameras.<ref name=cgmrev /><ref name=pcgamerus /> One Scouting Orb may be deployed at a time; when it lands, the player views the game world from its perspective until normal play is resumed.<ref name=manual /> The player can listen for noises, such as footsteps and humming, to determine the locations of enemies.<ref name=cgmrev /><ref name=manual /> On the highest of the game's three [[Balance (game design)#Difficulty level|difficulty levels]], killing humans results in a [[game over]],<ref name=manual /> and in certain missions the player must not knock out any guards.<ref name=nytimes />
{{Clear}}

==Plot==
===Setting and characters===
Like its predecessor ''[[Thief: The Dark Project]]'', ''Thief II'' is set in a [[steampunk]] metropolis called the City,<ref name=manual /><ref name=ignretro /> whose appearance resembles that of both medieval and [[Victorian era]] cities.<ref name=ignretro>{{cite web | last=Doke | first=Shunal | title=Thieving Through the Ages | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140220095825/http://in.ign.com/en/feature/1586/thief-a-look-at-the-past | url=http://in.ign.com/en/feature/1586/thief-a-look-at-the-past | date=February 20, 2014 | work=[[IGN]] | archive-date=February 20, 2014 }}</ref><ref name=pagliarulo /> Magic and steam technology exist side by side,<ref name=rpgvault /> and three factions—the manipulative and enigmatic Keepers, the technology-focused Hammerites and the "pagan" worshippers of the [[Pan (god)|Pan]]-like Trickster god—are in operation.<ref name=rpgvault /><ref name=cgmprev2 /><ref name=ignprev18 /><ref name=kenlev>{{cite web | last=Weise | first=Matthew | title=Looking Glass Studios Interview Series - Audio Podcast 5 - Ken Levine | url=http://gambit.mit.edu/updates/2011/06/looking_glass_studios_intervie_4.php | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130401065258/http://gambit.mit.edu/updates/2011/06/looking_glass_studios_intervie_4.php | date=June 29, 2011 | archive-date=April 1, 2013 | work=Singapore-MIT GAMBIT Game Lab }}</ref> ''Thief II'' takes place one year after the first game.<ref name=pczoneprev /> In the aftermath of the Trickster's defeat and the failure of his plan to revert the world to a wild, primitive state,<ref name=cgmrev /><ref name=rpgvault /><ref>{{cite video game |title=Thief: The Dark Project |developer=Looking Glass Studios |publisher=Eidos Interactive |date=1998 |quote='''Trickster's Note:''' The world as I once knew it was a place of magic—full of mystery and inhabited by creatures of glamour and terror. The men who lived there lit their bonfires and wondered at what crept and lurked in the darkness outside their weak circles of light. All their dreams, their aspirations and dreads, come from that darkness. Now, as the forces of "progress" cover the meadows in brick and cobblestone, as they replace the majestic loft of tree with the blocky ponderousness of building, they also light the world in their electric, actinic glare. With the lighting of the shadows, man loses his ability to fear, and to dream. [...] I have conceived of a plan to revive the darkness, to bring a resurrection of the ability to fear and dream. }}</ref> a schism in the Hammerite religion spawns the "Mechanist" sect, which fanatically values technological progress.<ref name=rpgvault /><ref name=eurogamer /> The new inventions of the Mechanists are used by a resurgent police force to crack down on crime.<ref name=rpgvault /><ref name=pczoneprev /> The pagans are in disarray, and have been driven into the wilderness beyond the City.<ref name=cgmrev /><ref name=rpgvault /> From there, they engage in [[guerrilla warfare]] against the Mechanists.<ref name=rpgvault /> The Keeper faction is dormant as the game begins.<ref name=cgmrev />

The game continues the story of Garrett (voiced by [[Stephen Russell]]), the cynical master thief who defeated the Trickster.<ref name=cgwrev /><ref name=cgmrev /><ref name=manual /> Pursuing Garrett is the new sheriff, Gorman Truart (voiced by Sam Babbitt), who has imposed a [[zero tolerance]] policy on crime.<ref name=manual /><ref name=pczoneprev /> Viktoria (voiced by [[Terri Brosius]]), the former ally of the Trickster, eventually joins with Garrett to combat the Mechanists.<ref name=pczonerev /><ref name=tenspot>{{cite web | author=Staff | year=2000 | title=Readers' Choice - The Ten Best Female Characters | url=http://www.gamespot.com/features/tenspot_readers_females/index.html | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20010210004300/http://www.gamespot.com/features/tenspot_readers_females/index.html | work=[[GameSpot]] | archive-date=February 10, 2001 }}</ref> The game's primary antagonist is the founder of the Mechanists, Father Karras (also voiced by Russell), a mentally unstable inventor who despises the natural world.<ref name=pczonerev /><ref name=eurogamer>{{cite web | last=Dean | first=Paul | date=October 7, 2012 | title=''Thief 2: The Metal Age'' retrospective | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130112001157/http://www.eurogamer.net/articles/2012-10-07-thief-2-the-metal-age-retrospective | url=http://www.eurogamer.net/articles/2012-10-07-thief-2-the-metal-age-retrospective | archive-date=January 12, 2013 | work=[[Eurogamer]] }}</ref>

===Story===
The game begins as Garrett continues his life as a thief. However, he is betrayed by his fence and ambushed after an early mission, and he determines that Truart, the local sheriff, is hunting him.<ref name=cgwrev /> Keepers take Garrett to hear a prophecy about the "Metal Age",<ref>{{cite video game | title=Thief II: The Metal Age | date=March 23, 2000 | developer=Looking Glass Studios | publisher=Eidos Interactive | quote='''Garrett:''' Nice poem. / '''Keeper:''' Not poetry: prophecy. The Metal Age is upon us. }}</ref> which he ignores.<ref>{{cite video game | title=Thief II: The Metal Age | date=March 23, 2000 | developer=Looking Glass Studios | publisher=Eidos Interactive | quote='''Garrett:''' Well, you've got the danger part right anyway. Tell you what: you Keepers can plant a few shrubs about town and I'll take care of me. I'll find my own way home. }}</ref> As Garrett leaves, Artemus, the Keeper who brought him into the order, informs him that Truart had been hired to kill him,<ref>{{cite video game | title=Thief II: The Metal Age | date=March 23, 2000 | developer=Looking Glass Studios | publisher=Eidos Interactive | quote='''Keeper:''' You have trouble, my friend. Danger from someone who hired Truart to kill you. }}</ref> and he gives Garrett a letter that directs him to eavesdrop on a Mechanist meeting.<ref>{{cite video game | title=Thief II: The Metal Age | date=March 23, 2000 | developer=Looking Glass Studios | publisher=Eidos Interactive | quote='''Letter:''' If you seek the private knowledge of the Sheriff, go to the Eastport Mechanist seminary tomorrow night. With stealthy discretion, overhear what you may, at a certain very timely meeting. }}</ref> There, Garrett overhears Truart and Father Karras discussing the conversion of [[street people]] into mindless "Servants",<ref>{{cite video game | title=Thief II: The Metal Age | date=March 23, 2000 | developer=Looking Glass Studios | publisher=Eidos Interactive | quote='''Karras:''' Behold, Sheriff Truart! From the lowly street rot emerges the loyal worker. That which I call 'The Servant.' / '''Truart:''' This is one of the tramps I delivered to you? The transformation is spectacular! / '''Karras:''' And neither want nor worry has he. }}</ref> who wear masks that emit a red vapor capable of reducing themselves and any nearby organic material to rust.<ref>{{cite video game | title=Thief II: The Metal Age | date=March 23, 2000 | developer=Looking Glass Studios | publisher=Eidos Interactive | quote='''Karras:''' I must ask thee to step away from the Masked Servant. That's right. And meanwhile, I will retrieve our 'volunteer.' A most unfortunate guttersnipe who waits just outside. Come, come, gentle beggar. And stand ye just there, next to the masked man. [...] / '''Truart:''' My word! The mask emits a red vapor! [...] They're gone! And what remains in their stead? Sand? No--rust! }}</ref> Truart promises to provide Karras with twenty victims for the Servant project,<ref>{{cite video game | title=Thief II: The Metal Age | date=March 23, 2000 | developer=Looking Glass Studios | publisher=Eidos Interactive | quote='''Truart:''' You need subjects for your Servant project, and I can supply them. [[Vagrancy (people)|Vagabonds]], street scum, [[prostitute]]s: those who will not be missed by anyone of consequence. They'll be rounded up, charges invented, et cetera. Still, there's always risk. So I will give you twenty; no more. }}</ref> not realizing that Karras is recording his words for use in blackmail.<ref>{{cite video game | title=Thief II: The Metal Age | date=March 23, 2000 | developer=Looking Glass Studios | publisher=Eidos Interactive | quote='''Karras:''' Now, behold, my wax cylinder machine. I've used it to capture the Sheriff's very words, even as they moved through the air, today. [...] With his voice thus preserved, Truart dare not betray me or he'll have the scandal he fears so much. }}</ref> Garrett steals the recording from a [[safe deposit box]], in order to coerce Truart into revealing his employer.<ref>{{cite video game | title=Thief II: The Metal Age | date=March 23, 2000 | developer=Looking Glass Studios | publisher=Eidos Interactive | quote='''Garrett:''' That recording should let me exert a little pressure on Truart to find out who hired him to kill me. [...] The Mechanists put the recording in a safety deposit box earlier today but since I have a copy of the key, I should be able to open it. [...] It didn't take much to learn that the Mechanists do all their banking with First City Bank and Trust, one of the wealthiest establishments in town, catering to the financial needs of the city's upper crust. }}</ref>

However, when Garrett sneaks into Truart's estate to confront him, he finds Truart has been murdered.<ref>{{cite video game | title=Thief II: The Metal Age | date=March 23, 2000 | developer=Looking Glass Studios | publisher=Eidos Interactive | quote='''Garrett:''' Damn! Someone beat me to the Sheriff. I better keep a low profile or else I'll be pinned as the killer. }}</ref> Evidence at the crime scene leads him to spy on the [[police officer]] Lt. Mosley. Garrett sees Mosley deliver a suspicious letter, which is carried through a portal by a wounded pagan. Garrett enters the portal and finds himself outside the City,<ref>{{cite video game | title=Thief II: The Metal Age | date=March 23, 2000 | developer=Looking Glass Studios | publisher=Eidos Interactive | quote='''Garrett:''' The keyring I found at Truart's house belongs to Lt. Mosley of the City Watch[. ...] And sure enough, she just left the local Watch station well before schedule carrying a letter. This is my chance. If I can trail her without being spotted, I should be able to find who's on the other end of this little conspiracy. }}</ref><ref>{{cite video game | title=Thief II: The Metal Age | date=March 23, 2000 | developer=Looking Glass Studios | publisher=Eidos Interactive | quote='''Garrett:''' The portal from the graveyard deposited me in a grove of trees and the wounded pagan I was following is nowhere in sight. He's carrying Mosley's letter and I'd still like to know where he's heading with it. }}</ref> and he follows the pagan's trail of blood to Viktoria, who persuades Garrett to join her against the Mechanists.<ref>{{cite video game | title=Thief II: The Metal Age | date=March 23, 2000 | developer=Looking Glass Studios | publisher=Eidos Interactive | quote='''Garrett:''' I'm hoping he's in too much of a hurry to stop and tend to that wound so he'll leave a trail of blood that I can follow. }}</ref><ref>{{cite video game | title=Thief II: The Metal Age | date=March 23, 2000 | developer=Looking Glass Studios | publisher=Eidos Interactive | quote='''Viktoria:''' Sometimes enemies must join forces to overcome a more terrible foe. So tell me, Garrett, yes or no. Are we agreed to work together, sharing knowledge and skills against the Mechanists? / '''Garrett:''' I... agree...that.... }}</ref> On a lead from Viktoria, he infiltrates Karras' office to learn about the "Cetus Project",<ref>{{cite video game | title=Thief II: The Metal Age | date=March 23, 2000 | developer=Looking Glass Studios | publisher=Eidos Interactive | quote='''Viktoria:''' ...you must find out whatever you can about the Cetus Project, a name our agents have overheard repeatedly. Karras has an office in the tower. Try to obtain some information there. }}</ref> and inadvertently discovers that Karras is giving Servants to the City's nobles.<ref>{{cite video game | title=Thief II: The Metal Age | date=March 23, 2000 | developer=Looking Glass Studios | publisher=Eidos Interactive | quote='''Viktoria:''' You say he's giving these 'Servants' as gifts? / '''Garrett:''' Yes[. ...] The servants are weapons, and the nobles have just invited them into their homes. }}</ref> Garrett travels to a Mechanist base to find out more about the Cetus Project,<ref>{{cite video game | title=Thief II: The Metal Age | date=March 23, 2000 | developer=Looking Glass Studios | publisher=Eidos Interactive | quote='''Viktoria:''' And the schematics confirmed what my agents presumed: Markham's Isle is the staging area for the Cetus Project. }}</ref> which is revealed to be a [[submarine]]. In order to locate and kidnap a high-ranking Mechanist named Brother Cavador, Garrett stows away in the vehicle.<ref>{{cite video game | title=Thief II: The Metal Age | date=March 23, 2000 | developer=Looking Glass Studios | publisher=Eidos Interactive | quote='''Garrett:''' And now I know more about the Cetus Project than I ever wanted to. They've built a ship that can can sail underwater. [...] The only way I can reach him is to hitch a ride in its belly. [...] 'Course it's not enough just to find Brother Cavador at this mysterious "K.D. site", I said I'd bring him back in one piece. }}</ref>

After delivering Cavador to Viktoria, Garrett steals a Servant mask to learn about a Mechanist technology called a "Cultivator". Meanwhile, Karras hides inside the Mechanist cathedral in preparation for his plan.<ref>{{cite video game | title=Thief II: The Metal Age | date=March 23, 2000 | developer=Looking Glass Studios | publisher=Eidos Interactive | quote='''Viktoria:''' ...and some sort of agricultural device called a Cultivator. / [...] '''Garrett:''' I think I know where we can lay our hands on one of those masks. There's a collector named Bram Gervaisius with an interest in masks and headdresses. / [...] '''Viktoria:''' Gervaisius is planning an exhibition. He's bringing his collection with him from his summer home. / [...] '''Garrett:''' Karras is holed up inside the Mechanist cathedral and it looks like whatever he's up to, we're running out of time. }}</ref> Garrett and Viktoria learn that it is the Cultivators inside Servant masks which emit red vapor, or "rust gas". Karras had provided Servants to nobles with gardens in order to set off an [[Apocalypse|apocalyptic]] chain reaction.<ref>{{cite video game | title=Thief II: The Metal Age | date=March 23, 2000 | developer=Looking Glass Studios | publisher=Eidos Interactive | quote='''Viktoria:''' The reaction will continue if it finds more organic material. [...] Garrett, for what purpose would the Mechanists use these Cultivators? / '''Garrett:''' Well, we know Karras has installed them in the masks of servants. / [...] And the servants have been placed in the homes of the wealthy. / '''Viktoria:''' Yes! The homes with the gardens. The plants there could sustain a reaction large enough to destroy everything! }}</ref> Viktoria plans to lure the Servants into the [[Hermetic seal|hermetically sealed]] Mechanist cathedral before Karras activates their masks, but Garrett believes this to be too dangerous and leaves.<ref>{{cite video game | title=Thief II: The Metal Age | date=March 23, 2000 | developer=Looking Glass Studios | publisher=Eidos Interactive | quote='''Viktoria:''' We must go to the Mechanist cathedral. The beacon you've heard about, you could find it, try to activate it, to draw the servants to the cathedral! Then you must somehow get Karras to signal them, to release the rust gas! You see, if I fill the cathedral with plants, enough to fuel a chain reaction, then it should cause the same effect we just saw, but it would take Karras with it, instead of the City! / [...] '''Garrett:''' Your plan is suicide. I'll think of a better way. And I work alone. }}</ref> Viktoria goes to the cathedral alone and dies while filling it with plants,<ref>{{cite video game | title=Thief II: The Metal Age | date=March 23, 2000 | developer=Looking Glass Studios | publisher=Eidos Interactive | quote='''Keeper:''' Viktoria has begun an assault on the Mechanist cathedral. / [...] '''Viktoria:''' I'm plant enough! }}</ref> and Garrett completes her plan, killing Karras in the rust gas. Afterward, Garrett is approached by Artemus, who explains that Karras' scheme and Viktoria's death had been prophesied. Garrett demands to know the rest of the Keepers' prophecies as the game ends.<ref>{{cite video game | title=Thief II: The Metal Age | date=March 23, 2000 | developer=Looking Glass Studios | publisher=Eidos Interactive | quote='''Garrett:''' Viktoria's death... and Karras... was it written? In your books? / '''Keeper:''' All is... as it was written. / '''Garrett:''' And there's more? / '''Keeper:''' Yes. / '''Garrett:''' Tell me! }}</ref>

==Development==
===Early production===
Looking Glass Studios began designing ''Thief II'' in January 1999.<ref name=gasource /> The team's goal was to build on the foundation of ''Thief: The Dark Project'',<ref name=nextgen1>{{cite web|author=Staff |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20000129185104/http://www.next-generation.com/jsmid/news/7240.html |url=http://www.next-generation.com/jsmid/news/7240.html |title=Looking Glass Talks ''Thief 2'' |archive-date=January 29, 2000 |date=July 30, 1999 |work=[[Next Generation (magazine)|Next Generation]] |url-status=dead }}</ref> a game that ''Thief II'' project director Steve Pearsall later said was an experiment.<ref name=rpgvault>{{cite web|last=Aihoshi |first=Richard |date=January 26, 2000 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20000815220921/http://rpgvault.ign.com/features/interviews/thief2.shtml |url=http://rpgvault.ign.com/features/interviews/thief2.shtml |title=''Thief 2: The Metal Age'' Interview |archive-date=August 15, 2000 |work=[[Vault Network]] |url-status=dead }}</ref> He explained that the team had played it safe by including certain "exploration ... or adventure oriented" missions with "jumping and climbing puzzles" in ''Thief'',<ref name=ignprev18 /><ref name=gamespyint>{{cite web | last=Harris | first=Tricia | title=Steve Pearsall of Looking Glass Studios | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20000303161334/http://www.gamespy.com/interviews/pearsall_a.shtm | url=http://www.gamespy.com/interviews/pearsall_a.shtm | date=February 5, 2000 | work=[[GameSpy]] | archive-date=March 3, 2000 }}</ref> and that the new game was significantly more focused on stealth.<ref name=rpgvault /><ref name=pczoneprev>{{cite journal | last=Pullin | first=Keith | title=''Thief II: The Metal Age'' | date=March 2000 | issue=87 | journal=[[PC Zone]] | pages=42–47 }}</ref> Combat was given less prominence than in the original.<ref name=pagliarulo /><ref name=pczoneprev /> Based on feedback from players and reviewers of ''Thief'',<ref name=pagliarulo /><ref name=pczoneprev /> the team decided to scale back the use of maze-like levels and monsters such as [[zombie]]s in favor of urban environments and human enemies.<ref name=pagliarulo /><ref name=nextgen1 /><ref name=checkout>{{cite web|last=Jensen |first=Chris |date=March 4, 2000 |title=''Thief II'': Exclusive Interview with James Poole |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20010111145900/http://www.checkout.com/games/features/info/0%2C%2C1875232-1%2C00.html |url=http://www.checkout.com/games/features/info/0,,1875232-1,00.html |work=CheckOut |archive-date=January 11, 2001 |url-status=dead }}</ref> Pearsall stated that ''Thief''{{'}}s monsters were negatively received because, unlike the game's human enemies, they did not clearly indicate when they noticed the player. The team sought to remedy this problem by improving the audio cues given by non-human enemies in the sequel.<ref name=gasource>{{cite web|last=Bergerud |first=John |title=Steve Pearsall, Project Director on ''Thief II'' |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/19991010012428/http://www.ga-source.com/interviews/thief2.shtml |url=http://www.ga-source.com/interviews/thief2.shtml |work=GA-Source |archive-date=October 10, 1999 |date=July 18, 1999 |url-status=dead }}</ref>

Production of ''Thief II'' commenced in February.<ref name=ignprev1 /> Looking Glass chose to compose the game's team of "half the original designers and half new blood", according to executive producer James Poole.<ref name=checkout /> The company tried to select people who meshed well both personally and creatively, in an attempt to guarantee a smooth development cycle.<ref name=gamespyint /> [[Adrenaline Vault]] editor-in-chief [[Emil Pagliarulo]] was hired as a junior designer, in part because of his positive review of ''Thief''.<ref name=fallout>{{cite web |author=Staff |title=GDC 2009: ''Fallout 3'' lead opens game design vault |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140219192847/http://www.gamespot.com/articles/gdc-2009-fallout-3-lead-opens-game-design-vault/1100-6206965/ |url=http://www.gamespot.com/articles/gdc-2009-fallout-3-lead-opens-game-design-vault/1100-6206965/ |url-status=live |work=[[GameSpot]] |date=March 27, 2009 |archive-date=February 19, 2014 }}</ref> Rich "zdim" Carlson and [[Iikka Keränen]] joined from [[Ion Storm]]'s ''[[Daikatana]]'' team, and Looking Glass contractor [[Terri Brosius]] was hired as a full-time designer.<ref name=rpgvault /><ref name=thief2doc /> One-third of the team was female, which Pearsall believed contributed to a strong [[group dynamics|group dynamic]]. As was typical at Looking Glass, the ''Thief II'' team worked in a wall-less space called a "pit", which allowed them to converse easily.<ref name=gamespyint /> Describing the work environment at the time, writer Laura Baldwin noted that "conversations dash madly about the room, [and] when someone is demonstrating something interesting everyone gravitates over to look."<ref name=ttlgint />

During the first months of development, the team regularly gathered to watch films pertinent to Garrett's character and to the game's visual design, such as ''[[The Third Man]]'', ''[[The Castle of Cagliostro]]'', ''[[M (1931 film)|M]]'' and ''[[Metropolis (1927 film)|Metropolis]]''.<ref name=pagliarulo /><ref name=ignprev1>{{cite web | last=Bates | first=Jason | date=May 13, 1999 | title=''Thief 2: The Metal Age'' E3 Update | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/19991013041000/http://pc.ign.com/previews/11726.html | url=http://pc.ign.com/previews/11726.html | archive-date=October 13, 1999 | url-status=dead | work=[[IGN]] }}</ref><ref name=ttlgint>{{cite web | title=''Thief 2'' Development Team TTLG Exclusive Interview | date=November 17, 1999 | work=Through the Looking Glass | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120305173933/http://www.ttlg.com/articles/t2interview/default.asp | archive-date=March 5, 2012 | url=http://www.ttlg.com/articles/t2interview/default.asp }}</ref> Pearsall said that the latter two films were ''Thief II''{{'}}s "biggest aesthetic influences", while the main inspiration for its plot was [[Umberto Eco]]'s novel ''[[The Name of the Rose]]''.<ref name=ttlgint /> The team also drew influence from [[Fritz Leiber]]'s ''[[Fafhrd and the Gray Mouser]]''.<ref name=rpgvault /> The game's story was written in the [[three-act structure]]: Garrett was intended to transition from his "cynical self" in the first act to a [[private investigator]] in the second, and to a character similar to [[James Bond]] in the third.<ref name=pagliarulo /><ref name=cgmprev2>{{cite web|last=Sones |first=Benjamin E. |title=''Thief 2'' |url=http://www.cdmag.com/articles/026/017/thief2_preview.html |work=[[Computer Games Magazine]] |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20030228113821/http://www.cdmag.com/articles/026/017/thief2_preview.html |archive-date=February 28, 2003 |date=February 4, 2000 |url-status=dead }}</ref> The City's technology and architecture were influenced by the appearance of Victorian London, and certain areas were given an [[Art Deco]] theme to provide "sort of a {{'}}''Batman''{{'}} feel", in reference to the [[Batman (1989 film)|1989 film]].<ref name=pagliarulo /> Lead artist Mark Lizotte captured over two-thousand photographs during his vacation in Europe,<ref name=ignprev18>{{cite web | last=Ward | first=Trent C. | date=October 20, 1999 | title=''Thief 2: The Metal Age'' | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/19991117141802/http://pc.ign.com/previews/11726.html | url=http://pc.ign.com/previews/11726.html | archive-date=November 17, 1999 | url-status=dead | work=[[IGN]] }}</ref><ref name=thief2doc /> and these were the basis for many of the game's [[Texture mapping|textures]].<ref name=cgmprev2 />

''Thief II'' was built with the third iteration of the [[Dark Engine]], which had been used previously for ''Thief'' and ''[[System Shock 2]]''.<ref name=pagliarulo>{{cite web | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20000119115317/http://www.avault.com/articles/getarticle.asp?name=thief2int&page=1 | url=http://www.avault.com/articles/getarticle.asp?name=thief2int&page=1 | title=Emerging From the Shadows: ''Thief 2'' Developer Interview | last=Laprad | first=David | date=July 28, 1999 | work=Adrenaline Vault | archive-date=January 19, 2000 }}</ref><ref name=pczoneprev /> According to Pearsall, the Dark Engine had become "a very well understood development environment", which made for an easier production process.<ref name=gamespyint /> Engine updates created for ''System Shock 2'', such as support for [[High color|16-bit color]], were carried over to ''Thief II''. The average [[3D modeling|character model]] in ''Thief II'' was given close to double the [[Polygon (computer graphics)|polygons]] of the average model in ''Thief'', with much of the added detail focused on characters' heads. This was an attempt to give the characters a "more organic" look.<ref name=cgmprev2 /> Certain [[artificial intelligence]] (AI) routines written into the Dark Engine, which allowed enemies to notice changes in the environment such as open doors, had not been used in ''Thief'' or in ''System Shock 2 ''but were implemented in ''Thief II''.<ref name=gasource /> Weather effects such as fog and rain were added,<ref name=cgmprev2 /> and technology from ''[[Flight Unlimited III]]'' was used to generate the sky and clouds.<ref name=pczoneprev />

===Announcement and continued development===
''Thief II'' was announced during the [[Electronic Entertainment Expo]] on May 13, 1999, as part of a contract between Looking Glass and [[Eidos Interactive]] to release four new games in the [[Thief (series)|''Thief'' series]], beginning with ''Thief Gold''.<ref name=businesswire>{{cite press release | title=Eidos Interactive Announces {{'}}''Thief II: The Metal Age''{{'}} | date=May 13, 1999 | location=Los Angeles | work=[[Business Wire]] }}</ref><ref name=avaulte3>{{cite web | last=Laprad | first=David | date=May 13, 1999 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20000817185258/http://avault.com/e3-1999/ | url=http://avault.com/e3-1999/ | title=E3 - DAY 1 | work=The Adrenaline Vault | archive-date=August 17, 2000 }}</ref> The deal had been signed on May 7, roughly three months after ''Thief II'' entered production.<ref name=ignprev1 /> A [[Technology demonstration|tech demo]] of the game, which Bruce Geryk of [[Games Domain]] described as "about three rooms with some Mages", was displayed on the show floor.<ref name=cgmprev2 /><ref name=gd>{{cite web|last=Geryk |first=Bruce |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20000420111735/http://www.gamesdomain.com/e3/thief2.html |url=http://www.gamesdomain.com/e3/thief2.html |title=''Thief 2: The Metal Age'' |work=[[Games Domain]] |date=May 15, 1999 |archive-date=April 20, 2000 |url-status=dead }}</ref> The demo was used to showcase the updated Dark Engine, which featured support for colored lighting, higher polygon models and larger environments.<ref name=nextgen1 /><ref name=gd /> The team revealed their intention to include more levels with human enemies,<ref name=nextgen1 /> and announced a projected release date of spring 2000.<ref name=gd /><ref name=cgmprev1>{{cite web|last=Sones |first=Benjamin E. |title=''Thief 2: The Metal Age'' First Look |url=http://www.cdmag.com/articles/020/123/thief2_fl.html |work=[[Computer Games Magazine]] |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20030703064245/http://www.cdmag.com/articles/020/123/thief2_fl.html |archive-date=July 3, 2003 |date=June 13, 1999 |url-status=dead }}</ref> Plans to include a [[Cooperative video game|cooperative multiplayer]] mode were also detailed at the show.<ref name=gd /> [[IGN]]'s Jason Bates noted that the ''Thief II'' display attracted "a bit of a buzz and a small crowd of dedicated onlookers".<ref name=ignprev1 />

By July, the team had begun initial construction of the game's levels.<ref name=gasource /> ''Thief II''{{'}}s increased focus on stealth necessitated new level design concepts: the most stealth-based missions in ''Thief'' had centered on urban [[burglary]], but Pearsall explained that this "would get tired pretty fast" if repeated in every level. The team diversified ''Thief II'' by designing missions with such objectives as kidnapping, blackmail and eavesdropping.<ref name=rpgvault /> The first two levels were designed to seamlessly introduce new players to the core [[game mechanics]], without a [[tutorial]] mission that might lose the interest of experienced players.<ref name=cgmprev2 /> When creating a mission, the team would often begin by deciding on the player's objective, after which they would produce a rough [[level design]]. The mission would then undergo a [[peer review]] to determine if it should be added to the game.<ref name=checkout /> Each of the game's levels was a team effort rather than the work of a single designer.<ref name=pagliarulo /> Designer [[Randy Smith (game designer)|Randy Smith]] explained that, while ''Thief''{{'}}s levels had been designed to fit a pre-existing story, the ''Thief II'' team "tried to think of really good missions first" and then adjusted the plot to suit them. He noted that it was highly difficult to harmonize the two.<ref name=thief2doc>{{cite AV media | people = Galpern, Fred (Producer, Director, Editor); Thron, Dan (Camera Operator) | year = 1999 | title = The Making of ''Thief II'' | location = Cambridge, Massachusetts | publisher = Looking Glass Studios }}</ref>

The game's sound team was composed of Kemal Amarasingham, [[Ramin Djawadi]] and audio director [[Eric Brosius]].<ref name=manual /><ref name=makingof /> According to Brosius, each member of the audio department did "everything", without clear demarcations between roles.<ref name=makingof /> Like ''Thief'', ''Thief II'' features a sound engine that simulates [[Sound#Propagation|propagation]] in real-time.<ref name=cgmprev2 /><ref name=gamespyt3>{{cite web | last=Sharp | first=Brian | title=''Thief: Deadly Shadows'' - Volume I | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20051226231927/http://pc.gamespy.com/pc/thief-deadly-shadows/508760p1.html | url=http://pc.gamespy.com/pc/thief-deadly-shadows/508760p1.html | work=[[GameSpy]] | date=April 24, 2004 | archive-date=December 26, 2005 }}</ref> To achieve this effect, each level's geometry was input both to the [[level editor]] and to a "separate [sound] database", which mapped how sound would realistically propagate based on "the physical room characteristics [... and] how all the different rooms and areas are connected together".<ref name=cgmprev2 /> For example, noise travels freely through an open door but is blocked when the door is closed.<ref name=gamespyt3 /> The team used the new "occlusion" feature in [[Environmental Audio Extensions|EAX]] 2.0 to make ''Thief II''{{'}}s sound environment more realistic and to allow the player to listen through doors.<ref name=gasource /> The game features more sound effects, music and speech than the original ''Thief''.<ref name=rpgvault /><ref name=pczoneprev /> ''Thief II''{{'}}s [[Video game music|score]], as with that of its predecessor, was designed to "blur ambient [sound] and music" together. However, Brosius later stated that, while ''Thief''{{'}}s soundtrack is composed of "simple and hypnotic" loops only a few seconds in length, ''Thief II'' features longer and "more thoughtfully" constructed pieces. He believed that this method had positive aspects, but that it resulted in a less immersive audio environment.<ref name=brosius2>{{cite web | last=Weise | first=Matthew | title=Looking Glass Studios Interview Series - Audio Podcast 7 - Eric Brosius | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130401035308/http://gambit.mit.edu/updates/2011/07/_part_7_of_a.php | url=http://gambit.mit.edu/updates/2011/07/_part_7_of_a.php | archive-date=April 1, 2013 | publisher=Singapore-MIT GAMBIT Game Lab | date=July 27, 2011 | url-status=live }}</ref>

Artist Dan Thron returned to create the game's cutscenes, with assistance from Jennifer Hrabota-Lesser.<ref name=pczoneprev /><ref name=makingof /> Thron later called Hrabota-Lesser "one of the greatest artists I've ever seen".<ref name=brosius /> The cutscenes, which ''[[Computer Games Magazine]]'' called "unique", feature multiple layers of artwork and footage of live actors filmed against a [[Chroma key|green screen]]. These components were combined and animated in [[Adobe After Effects]].<ref name=cgmprev2 /><ref name=makingof /> The technique had been developed for the original ''Thief'', as an evolution of designer [[Ken Levine (game developer)|Ken Levine]]'s suggestion to use [[motion comic]] cutscenes. [[David Lynch]]'s films ''[[Eraserhead]]'' and ''[[The Elephant Man (1980 film)|The Elephant Man]]'' were important influences on their style.<ref name=brosius>{{cite web|last=Weise |first=Matthew |date=January 18, 2012 |title=Looking Glass Studios Interview Series – Audio Podcast 9 – Terri Brosius and Dan Thron |url=http://gambit.mit.edu/updates/2012/01/looking_glass_studios_intervie_6.php |publisher=Singapore-MIT GAMBIT Game Lab |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130401071632/http://gambit.mit.edu/updates/2012/01/looking_glass_studios_intervie_6.php |archive-date=April 1, 2013 }}</ref>

===Final months===
By October 1999, the team had cut the game's multiplayer feature.<ref name=ignprev18 /> Pearsall explained that Looking Glass did not "have the resources to do a new kind of multiplayer and ship a finely tuned single-player game".<ref name=pczoneprev /> Plans were announced in January 2000 to release a multiplayer-only ''Thief'' game shortly after the completion of ''Thief II''.<ref name=ignprev20>{{cite web | last=Ward | first=Trent C. | title=''Thief 2: The Metal Age'' Preview | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20000817174442/http://pc.ign.com/previews/11726.html | url=http://pc.ign.com/previews/11726.html | work=[[IGN]] | archive-date=August 17, 2000 | url-status=dead | date=January 26, 2000 }}</ref> As ''Thief II''{{'}}s development continued, Looking Glass experienced extreme financial troubles. The company's [[Marc LeBlanc]] later said that "Eidos was writing a check every week to cover our burn rate" during the last months of the project. The game's final cost was roughly $2.5 million.<ref>{{cite web|first=Hiawatha|last=Bray|url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-boston-globe/141901598/|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20240223073529/https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-boston-globe/141901598/|title=Looking Glass closing, laying off 60 workers|newspaper=[[The Boston Globe]]|page=37|archivedate=February 23, 2024|date=May 26, 2000|accessdate=February 23, 2024|via=[[Newspapers.com]]}}</ref> According to company head [[Paul Neurath]], Eidos informed Looking Glass that "it was not an option" for ''Thief II'' to miss its release date, and that there would be "dire consequences if [we] missed by even a day". An anonymous Looking Glass staffer later told [[Salon.com]] that Eidos "told us basically to ship [''Thief II''] by their fiscal quarter or die".<ref name=salon>{{cite web |url=http://dir.salon.com/tech/feature/2000/06/20/dark_glass/ | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090428002554/http://dir.salon.com/tech/feature/2000/06/20/dark_glass/ | archive-date=April 28, 2009 | url-status=live | title=Game over | last=James Au | first=Wagner | date=June 20, 2000 | work=[[Salon.com]] }}</ref>

By January, Pearsall confirmed that the game had reached [[Software release life cycle#Beta|beta]], and that most of the team's energy was being spent "tuning, polishing, and fixing bugs".<ref name=rpgvault /> He noted in early February that ''Thief II'' had been produced almost entirely on schedule.<ref name=gamespyint /> The company slipped behind near the end of the project and entered [[wikt:crunch time|crunch time]] to make up the loss.<ref name=salon /> On February 24, ''Thief II'' producer Michael McHale announced that the game had reached "feature freeze", and that the team was in "super crunch mode". Numerous [[Game testing|game testers]] from Eidos joined the project. However, McHale said that the team was energized and that "spirits [were] high".<ref name=avault5>{{cite web | last=Laprad | first=David | title=''Thief 2'' Development Update | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20000412113505/http://www.avault.com/news/displaynews.asp?story=2242000-151549 | url=http://www.avault.com/news/displaynews.asp?story=2242000-151549 | archive-date=April 12, 2000 | work=The Adrenaline Vault | date=February 24, 2000 }}</ref> Certain employees slept in the office and avoided bathing so that the game could reach its March deadline. LeBlanc later stated his belief that the game was rushed, and that its quality suffered as a result. Nevertheless, the team met their goal,<ref name=salon /> and the game was released on March 23, 2000 in North America, and on March 31, 2000 in Europe.<ref name=cgmrelease>{{cite web|last=Fudge |first=James |title=''Thief II: The Metal Age'' Released |url=http://www.cdmag.com/articles/027/013/thief2.html |work=[[Computer Games Magazine]] |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20030525160533/http://www.cdmag.com/articles/027/013/thief2.html |archive-date=May 25, 2003 |date=March 23, 2000 |url-status=dead }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Gone Gold - European Releases |url=http://gonegold.com/golden/eurogold.shtml |access-date=2023-10-21 |archive-date=2000-12-14 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20001214134500/http://gonegold.com/golden/eurogold.shtml |url-status=bot: unknown }}</ref> Eidos expedited the company's payment for completing the game.<ref name=salon /><!--<ref name="t2cdmqt">{{cite web|last=Mayer|first=Robert|title=Thief II: The Metal Age: Raised on robbery|url=http://www.cdmag.com/articles/026/195/thief2_qt.html|work=[[Computer Games Magazine]] |access-date=November 15, 2010|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20030525173212/http://www.cdmag.com/articles/026/195/thief2_qt.html|archive-date=May 25, 2003|date=March 19, 2000}}</ref>-->

==Reception==
{{Video game reviews
| MC = 87/100<ref name="MC">{{cite web |url=https://www.metacritic.com/game/thief-ii-the-metal-age/critic-reviews/?platform=pc |title=Thief II: The Metal Age for PC Reviews |website=[[Metacritic]] |publisher=[[CBS Interactive]] |access-date=January 24, 2018}}</ref>
| CGM = 4.5/5<ref name=cgmrev>{{cite web|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20030517193120/http://www.cdmag.com/articles/027/051/thief2_review.html |url=http://www.cdmag.com/articles/027/051/thief2_review.html |title=''Thief 2: The Metal Age'' |date=April 4, 2000 |last=E. Sones |first=Benjamin |work=[[Computer Games Magazine|Computer Games Strategy Plus]] |archive-date=May 17, 2003 |url-status=dead }}</ref>
| CGW = 4.5/5<ref name=cgwrev />
| GameFan = 95 out of 100<ref name=gamefan />
| GamePro = 4 out of 5<ref name=gamepro>{{cite magazine | last=Brenesal | first=Barry | date=April 21, 2000 | title=''Thief II: The Metal Age'' | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20050212160534/http://www.gamepro.com/computer/pc/games/reviews/5307.shtml | url=http://www.gamepro.com/computer/pc/games/reviews/5307.shtml | archive-date=February 12, 2005 | magazine=[[GamePro]] }}</ref>
| NGen = 4/5<ref name="NG"/>
| PCGUS = 89%<ref name=pcgamerus />
| PCZone = 82%<ref name=pczonerev />
}}

''Thief 2'' debuted high on the bestsellers list for computer games,<ref name=salon /> and its initial sales were better than those of its commercially successful predecessor.<ref name=opii /> By November 2000, its global sales had surpassed 220,000 copies; ''PC Zone'' described these figures as "commercial acclaim".<ref name=pczonesales>{{cite journal| title=Ion Storm Steals ''Thief'' | author=Staff | journal=[[PC Zone]] | date=November 2000 | issue=95 | page=23 }}</ref> The United States alone accounted for 67,084 sales by the end of 2000, which drew in revenues of $2.37&nbsp;million.<ref name=pcgsales>{{cite journal |date=April 2000 |volume=8 |issue=4 |title=It's All in the Numbers |journal=[[PC Gamer]] |publisher=[[Future US]] |pages=40, 41 }}</ref> The game later received a "Silver" sales award by the [[Entertainment and Leisure Software Publishers Association]] (ELSPA),<ref name=silverelspa>{{cite web |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090221154943/http://www.elspa.com/?i=3942 |url=http://www.elspa.com:80/?i=3942 |title=ELSPA Sales Awards: Silver |work=[[Entertainment and Leisure Software Publishers Association]] |archive-date=February 21, 2009 |url-status=dead }}</ref> indicating sales of at least 100,000 copies in the United Kingdom.<ref name=gamasutrasales>{{cite web |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170918063107/https://www.gamasutra.com/view/news/112220/ELSPA_Wii_Fit_Mario_Kart_Reach_Diamond_Status_In_UK.php |url=https://www.gamasutra.com/view/news/112220/ELSPA_Wii_Fit_Mario_Kart_Reach_Diamond_Status_In_UK.php |title=ELSPA: ''Wii Fit'', ''Mario Kart'' Reach Diamond Status In UK |author=Caoili, Eric | date=November 26, 2008 |work=[[Gamasutra]] |archive-date=September 18, 2017 |url-status=dead }}</ref> ''Thief&nbsp;II'' also received positive reviews from critics, with an aggregate score of 87/100 on [[Metacritic]].<ref name="MC" />

''[[Computer Gaming World]]''{{'}}s Thomas L. McDonald wrote that "everything in ''Thief&nbsp;II'' is bigger, sharper, better, and more effective" than in its predecessor. He enjoyed its story and called its levels "vast and intricate", with "astonishingly complex and often beautiful" architecture; but he found the game's graphics to be somewhat lackluster. McDonald summarized ''Thief&nbsp;II'' as a unique "gamer's game".<ref name=cgwrev /> Jim Preston of ''[[PC Gamer US]]'' considered the game to be "more focused and polished than the original" and praised the removal of "zombie battles". While he faulted its graphics, he summarized it as "one hell of a good game".<ref name=pcgamerus>{{cite web |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20011228220820/http://www.pcgamer.com/reviews/review_2000-08-10al.html |url=http://www.pcgamer.com/reviews/review_2000-08-10al.html |last=Preston |first=Jim |date=August 2000 |title=''Thief II: The Metal Age'' |archive-date=December 28, 2001 |work=[[PC Gamer US]] |url-status=dead }}</ref>

Jasen Torres of ''[[GameFan]]'' wrote: "If you liked ''Thief'', you'll love ''Thief&nbsp;2: The Metal Age''; it's more of the stuff that made ''Thief'' great, with less of the annoying stuff". He applauded the removal of "zombie killer" missions and believed the game's sound to be "superior to any other game". He considered its story to be "good" but "nothing great" and its graphics to be "decent"; but he commented that the game was "really all about the gameplay", which he praised as "quite compelling and fun".<ref name=gamefan>{{cite web | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20000606163147/http://www.gamefan.com/repre.asp?g=1835&t=r | url=http://www.gamefan.com/repre.asp?g=1835&t=r | title=Thief 2: The Metal Age | last=Torres | first=Jasen | work=[[GameFan]] | date=April 4, 2000 | archive-date=June 6, 2000 | access-date=November 14, 2010 }}</ref> Benjamin E.&nbsp;Sones of ''[[Computer Games Magazine]]'' considered the game's story to be "quite good", but he faulted Looking Glass for failing to detail the events of the first game for new players. He wrote that ''Thief&nbsp;II''{{'}}s graphics were passable but that its sound design was "phenomenal". Sones praised its missions as "very well crafted" and noted that they gave the impression of being in "a living, breathing world". He summarized: "It may not be perfect, but ''Thief&nbsp;2'' has got it where it counts".<ref name=cgmrev />

Charles Harold of ''[[The New York Times]]'' called the game a "refreshing alternative to games that glorify violence". He found its story to be "slight", but he lauded its world as "amazingly alive" and its AI as a "remarkable impersonation of real intelligence".<ref name=nytimes>{{cite web | last=Herold | first=Charles | date=July 6, 2000 | url=https://select.nytimes.com/gst/abstract.html?res=F10A14F83A5D0C758CDDAE0894D8404482 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110214213134/http://www.nytimes.com/2000/07/06/technology/game-theory-thief-ii-stresses-stealth-over-strength.html | archive-date=February 14, 2011 | title=GAME THEORY; ''Thief II'' Stress Stealth Over Strength | work=[[The New York Times]] | access-date=April 11, 2011 }}</ref> Writing for ''[[GamePro]]'', Barry Brenesal commented that ''Thief&nbsp;II'' "provides a solid gaming experience" but "doesn't startle like its predecessor". He wrote that its missions featured a "great deal of variety" and praised their "ability to casually suggest a much larger world", but complained that they were linear. He considered the game's writing to be "among the best in the business". While Brenesal enjoyed the game's textures and lighting, he noted the low detail of the game's human models, whose animations he found to be "arthritic".<ref name=gamepro /> ''[[PC Zone]]''{{'}}s Paul Presley wrote that the game's levels were larger but easier than those of ''Thief'', and he considered their objectives to be somewhat linear. He found ''Thief&nbsp;II''{{'}}s graphics to be dated and wrote that its lack of real-time lighting "tends to give each environment a sort of 'false' quality". However, he believed that the game "still has enough atmosphere to immerse you" and praised its sound design. Presley considered the game to be a straightforward rehash of its predecessor and finished: "A more clear-cut case of sequel-itis there has never been."<ref name=pczonerev />

Jim Preston reviewed the PC version of the game for ''[[Next Generation (magazine)|Next Generation]]'', rating it four stars out of five, and stated that "Great, skulking gameplay, useful new tools, and clever level design make ''Thief&nbsp;II'' an excellent first-person 'sneaker'."<ref name="NG">{{cite magazine |last=Preston |first=Jim |title=Finals |magazine=[[Next Generation (magazine)|Next Generation]] |volume=3 |issue=6 |publisher=[[Future US|Imagine Media]] |date=June 2000 |page=104}}</ref>

==Post-release==
While ''Thief II'' performed well commercially, Looking Glass was not set to receive royalties for several months.<ref name=salon /><ref name=opii>{{cite web | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20000816001839/http://www.gamespy.com/interviews/lookingglass_a.shtm |url=http://www.gamespy.com/interviews/lookingglass_a.shtm |title=Once more through the Looking Glass |last=Opii |first=Valoria | year=2000 |work=[[GameSpy]] |archive-date=August 16, 2000 }}</ref> The company had struggled financially since the commercial failures of its self-published games ''[[Terra Nova: Strike Force Centauri]]'' and ''[[British Open Championship Golf]]''. Looking Glass's ''[[Flight Unlimited III]]'' had flopped at retail, and the development of ''[[Jane's Attack Squadron]]'' had gone over budget and fallen behind schedule. A deal to co-develop the stealth game ''Deep Cover'' with [[Irrational Games]] had recently collapsed.<ref name=opii /><ref name=maximumpc>{{cite journal | journal=[[Maximum PC]] | title=Game Theory; Beyond the Looking Glass |date=August 2000 | page=31 | author=McDonald, T. Liam}}</ref><ref name=sterrett>{{cite web | last=Sterrett | first=James | url=http://www.ttlg.com/articles/lgsclosing2.asp | url-status=live | archive-date=March 8, 2014 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140308015222/http://www.ttlg.com/articles/lgsclosing2.asp | title=Reasons for the Fall: A Post-Mortem On Looking Glass Studios | date=May 31, 2000 | publisher=Through the Looking Glass }}</ref> According to Looking Glass's Tim Stellmach, the delay in ''Thief II'' royalties "faced [us] with the prospect of running out of money."<ref name=opii /> Looking Glass management signed a deal in which Eidos Interactive would acquire the company, but Eidos fell into a sudden financial crisis, in part because of the failure of [[Ion Storm]]'s $40 million game ''[[Daikatana]]''.<ref name=salon /><ref name=opii /><ref name=maximumpc /><ref name=sterrett /> These factors led to the closure of Looking Glass on May 24, 2000,<ref name=cgw5>{{cite magazine | last=Asher | first=Mark | title=read.me; Looking Glass Shuts Down | magazine=[[Computer Gaming World]] | date=August 2000 | issue=193 }}</ref> with the planned ''Thief II'' successors ''Thief II Gold'' and ''Thief III'' cancelled.<ref name=salon /><ref name=opii />

===Later installments===
{{Main|Thief: Deadly Shadows|Thief (2014 video game)}}
The ''Thief'' series had been planned as a trilogy,<ref name=salon /> and work on ''Thief III'' was "in a fairly advanced stage" when Looking Glass closed, according to ''PC Zone''{{'}}s Keith Pullin.<ref name=pczonet32>{{cite journal | last=Pullin | first=Keith | title=The great game robbery; ''Thief 3'' | date=July 2003 | issue=130 | journal=[[PC Zone]] | pages=36–39 }}</ref> Randy Smith and Terri Brosius were appointed as lead designers, and they developed the game's concept over several months.<ref name=smith3>{{cite web | last=Weise | first=Matthew | title=Looking Glass Studios Interview Series - Audio Podcast 4 - Randy Smith | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130401070322/http://gambit.mit.edu/updates/2011/06/looking_glass_studios_intervie_3.php | url=http://gambit.mit.edu/updates/2011/06/looking_glass_studios_intervie_3.php | archive-date=April 1, 2013 | publisher=Singapore-MIT GAMBIT Game Lab | date=June 22, 2011 | url-status=live }}</ref> In an open letter published after the company's bankruptcy, Smith wrote that the third game would have taken place in an "open-ended, self-directed city", and that its plot would have centered on the Keepers.<ref name=gamespynews>{{cite web | last=Keefer | first=John | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20000621233650/http://www.gamespy.com/news/May00/5-24-00-1.shtm | url=http://www.gamespy.com/news/May00/5-24-00-1.shtm | title=Looking Glass Studios closes down | date=May 24, 2000 | work=[[GameSpy]] | archive-date=June 21, 2000 }}</ref> Brosius suggested that ''Thief III'' would have seen Garrett "accept[ing] that there are consequences to his actions", and that he would likely have become "ready to give, rather than always take."<ref name=salon /> The player would have uncovered the game's story gradually, while exploring a [[Nonlinear gameplay|free-roam environment]].<ref name=pcgamerukt3 /> Serious plans had been made to include co-operative multiplayer,<ref name=pczoneprev /><ref name=checkout /> and a new engine, Siege, had been in production.<ref name=pcgamerukt3>{{cite magazine | last=Gillen | first=Kieron | author-link=Kieron Gillen | title=Ion Storm in Heaven: The Genesis of ''Deus Ex 2'' and ''Thief III'' | date=August 2001 | magazine=[[PC Gamer UK]] | pages=34–38 | issue=85 }}</ref> When Looking Glass closed, its assets were liquidated and the ''Thief'' intellectual property was sold at auction.<ref name=opii /><ref name=salon2>{{cite web |last=Au |first=Wagner James |title=Ion Storm catches ''Thief'' |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150518163826/http://www.salon.com/2000/08/10/thief_2/ |url=http://www.salon.com/2000/8/10/thief_2/ |url-status=live |work=[[Salon.com]] |date=10 August 2000 |archive-date=May 18, 2015 }}</ref> This raised doubts that the ''Thief'' trilogy would be completed,<ref name=salon /><ref name=gamespynews /> a situation that [[Salon.com]] writer Wagner James Au compared to [[Lucasfilm]] closing after the release of ''[[The Empire Strikes Back]]''.<ref name=salon /> However, following rumors, Eidos announced on August 9, 2000 that it had purchased the rights to ''Thief''.<ref name=salon2 />

Development of ''Thief III'' was delegated to the [[Warren Spector]]-supervised Ion Storm, which had recently completed ''[[Deus Ex (video game)|Deus Ex]]''.<ref name=salon2 /><ref name=ttlgnews>{{cite press release | location=[[San Francisco]] | title=Eidos Interactive To Continue Critically Acclaimed ''Thief'' Franchise For The PC and PlayStation 2 Computer Entertainment System  | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20001102123415/http://www.ttlg.com/shownews.asp?id=381 | url= http://www.ttlg.com/shownews.asp?id=381 | archive-date=November 2, 2000 | date=August 8, 2000 | publisher=Eidos Interactive }}</ref> According to Spector, ''Thief III'' would have been given to [[Core Design]] or [[Crystal Dynamics]] had he not accepted it.<ref name=salon2 /> The game was announced for [[Microsoft Windows|Windows]] and the [[PlayStation 2]].<ref name=ttlgnews /> On August 10, Spector commented that Ion Storm's first goal was to assemble a core team, composed in part of former Looking Glass employees, to design and plot the game.<ref name=gamespott3>{{cite web|last=Parker |first=Sam |title=Eidos Confirms ''Thief 3'' Plans |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20000815094021/http://www.zdnet.com/gamespot/stories/news/0%2C10870%2C2613736%2C00.html |url=http://www.zdnet.com/gamespot/stories/news/0,10870,2613736,00.html |archive-date=August 15, 2000 |date=August 9, 2000 |work=[[GameSpot]] |url-status=dead }}</ref> ''Thief II'' team members Randy Smith, Lulu Lamer, Emil Pagliarulo and Terri Brosius were hired to begin the project.<ref name=pcgamerukt3 /><ref name=pcgamerust3>{{cite journal | last=Osborn | first=Chuck | title=After the ION Storm | date=August 2001 | volume=8 | issue=8 | journal=[[PC Gamer US]] | pages=37–42 }}</ref> On August 16, Ion Storm announced its hires, and stated that concept work on ''Thief III'' would begin in September.<ref name=gamespott32>{{cite web |last=Parker |first=Sam |date=August 16, 2000 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160110152139/http://www.gamespot.com/articles/thief-iii-team-update/1100-2616465/ |url=http://www.gamespot.com/articles/thief-iii-team-update/1100-2616465/ |title=''Thief III'' Team Update |work=[[GameSpot]] |archive-date=January 10, 2016 |url-status=dead }}</ref> The team planned to "wrap up [the] loose ends" of the series,<ref name=gamespott3 /> and they built directly upon the ''Thief III'' concept work done at Looking Glass.<ref name=smithrpg>{{cite web | author=Staff | title=''Thief 3'' Infobit | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20030729101429/http://rpgvaultarchive.ign.com/archive/arc43.shtml | url=http://rpgvaultarchive.ign.com/archive/arc43.shtml | work=[[Vault Network]] | date=December 5, 2000 | url-status=dead | archive-date=July 29, 2003 }}</ref> ''Thief III'' was eventually renamed ''[[Thief: Deadly Shadows]]'',<ref name=pczonet3>{{cite journal | last=Holden | first=Anthony | date=April 2004 | title=''Thief: Deadly Shadows'' | issue=140 | journal=[[PC Zone]] | pages=36–40 }}</ref> and it was released for Windows and the [[Xbox (console)|Xbox]] on May 25, 2004.<ref name=ignnewst3>{{cite web | last=Adams | first=David | title=''Thief: Deadly Shadows'' Ships | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20050306065018/http://pc.ign.com/articles/518/518908p1.html | url=http://pc.ign.com/articles/518/518908p1.html | archive-date=March 6, 2005 | work=[[IGN]] | url-status=dead | date=May 25, 2004 }}</ref>

In May 2009, after several months of rumors, a fourth game in the ''Thief'' series was announced by ''[[Deus Ex: Human Revolution]]'' developer [[Eidos-Montréal]].<ref name=rps>{{cite web | last=Rossignol | first=Jim | title=4 Real: ''Thief 4'' | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090516191846/http://www.rockpapershotgun.com/2009/05/11/4-real-thief-4/ | url=http://www.rockpapershotgun.com/2009/05/11/4-real-thief-4/ | archive-date=May 16, 2009 | date=May 11, 2009 | work=[[Rock, Paper, Shotgun]] | url-status=live }}</ref> It was unveiled in the April 2013 issue of ''[[Game Informer]]''.<ref name=ignt4>{{cite web | last=MacDonald | first=Keza | title=''Thief 4'' Coming in 2014 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130308093038/http://www.ign.com/articles/2013/03/05/thief-4-coming-in-2014 | url=http://www.ign.com/articles/2013/03/05/thief-4-coming-in-2014 | archive-date=March 8, 2013 | url-status=live | date=March 5, 2013 | work=[[IGN]] }}</ref> The game, entitled ''[[Thief (2014 video game)|Thief]]'', is a reboot of the ''Thief'' series; and it does not feature the Hammerites, pagans or Keepers.<ref name=telegraph>{{cite web |last=Martin |first=Tim |title=''Thief'' review |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140429034623/http://www.telegraph.co.uk/technology/video-games/video-game-reviews/10658395/Thief-review.html |url=https://www.telegraph.co.uk/technology/video-games/video-game-reviews/10658395/Thief-review.html |work=[[The Daily Telegraph]] |archive-date=April 29, 2014 |url-status=live |date=February 24, 2014 }}</ref> Its plot follows Garrett (voiced by [[Romano Orzari]] in place of Stephen Russell) in the aftermath of an accident that leaves his protégé, Erin, missing. Garrett has amnesia after this incident, and the City is beset by a plague called the Gloom.<ref name=arstechnica>{{cite web | last=Orland | first=Kyle | title=Review: ''Thief'' reboot should have stayed hidden | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140307111749/http://arstechnica.com/gaming/2014/02/review-thief-reboot-should-have-stayed-hidden/ | url=https://arstechnica.com/gaming/2014/02/review-thief-reboot-should-have-stayed-hidden/ | work=[[Ars Technica]] | date=February 24, 2014 | archive-date=March 7, 2014 | url-status=live }}</ref><ref name=escapist>{{cite web | last=Young | first=Shamus | title=10 Great Things About the ''Thief'' Reboot | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140314123637/http://www.escapistmagazine.com/articles/view/columns/experienced-points/11096-10-Great-Things-About-the-Thief-Reboot | url=http://www.escapistmagazine.com/articles/view/columns/experienced-points/11096-10-Great-Things-About-the-Thief-Reboot | work=[[The Escapist (magazine)|The Escapist]] | date=March 11, 2014 | archive-date=March 14, 2014 | url-status=live }}</ref> The game was released for [[Microsoft Windows|Windows]] and the [[Xbox 360]], [[PlayStation 3]], [[Xbox One]] and [[PlayStation 4]] in February 2014.<ref name=ignt42>{{cite web | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140322023652/http://www.ign.com/games/thief-4 | url=http://www.ign.com/games/thief-4 | title=''Thief'' on IGN | work=[[IGN]] | archive-date=March 22, 2014 | url-status=live }}</ref>

===Fan expansion===
Soon after the bankruptcy of Looking Glass, a fan group called the Dark Engineering Guild began developing an expansion [[Mod (video gaming)|mod]] to ''Thief II'', entitled ''Thief 2X: Shadows of the Metal Age''.<ref name=pcgamer2x /><ref name=jolt>{{cite web | author=Staff | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20051110103759/http://www.jolt.co.uk/index.php?articleid=4606 | url=http://www.jolt.co.uk/index.php?articleid=4606 | title=Mod Spotlight: ''Thief 2X: Shadows of the Metal Age'' | date=September 18, 2005 | work=[[Jolt Online Gaming]] | archive-date=November 10, 2005 }}</ref> Initially, they hoped to fill the void left by the cancellation of ''Thief III'',<ref name=jolt /> but they continued to work on the mod after the announcement and release of ''Thief: Deadly Shadows''.<ref name=jolt /><ref name=pcgameruk2x /> Released in 2005 after five years in development, the mod follows Zaya, a young woman who is robbed while visiting the City and who then seeks revenge.<ref name=pcgamer2x /><ref name=jolt /><ref name=pcgameruk2x /><ref name=gameinformer2x /> She is mentored by a pagan hermit named Malak, who trains her as a thief but who has ulterior motives.<ref name=makingof>{{Cite AV media | author=Dark Engineering Guild | title=''T2X'' Making Of | date=September 2008 | at=Coverdisc | work=[[PC Gamer UK]] | issue=193 }}</ref> The team designed Zaya to be physically capable and to have a "middle-eastern/north-African look", but made an effort to avoid similarities to [[Mulan (Disney character)|Mulan]].<ref name=makingof /> Chronologically, the story starts near the end of ''Thief'' and ends in the middle of ''Thief II'', thereby depicting the rise of Gorman Truart and the early days of the Mechanists.<ref name=makingof /><ref name=jolt /> ''Thief 2X'' features 13 missions, with new animated cutscenes and roughly 3,000 new lines of recorded dialogue.<ref name=pcgamer2x>{{cite journal | last=Todd | first=Brett | title=Like Seagulls and 747s | date=October 2007 | volume=14 | issue=11 | journal=[[PC Gamer US]] | page=98 }}</ref><ref name=gameinformer2x>{{cite magazine | author=Staff | title=The Love of the Fans | date=December 2008 | issue=188 | magazine=[[Game Informer]] | page=137 }}</ref>

The mod was praised by critics and by the ''Thief'' fan community.<ref name=gameinformer2x /> Brett Todd of ''[[PC Gamer US]]'' awarded it "Mod of the Month" and wrote: "It doesn't quite have the mysterious allure of the original games, but it's awfully close".<ref name=pcgamer2x /> A writer for [[Jolt Online Gaming]] praised the mod's visuals and considered its missions to be "incredibly well designed". While the writer commented that ''Thief 2X'' did not perfectly follow the series' tone and that its voice acting was "not the best", they finished by saying that fans of the ''Thief'' series had "no excuse not to play ''T2X''".<ref name=jolt /> ''PC Gamer UK''{{'}}s [[Kieron Gillen]] wrote that he had expected the mod to be cancelled, given that the "web is full of [...] five-percent finished masterworks from people who aimed far, far too high". After ''Thief 2X''{{'}}s release, he lauded it as the best ''Thief'' fan work and as "one of the most impressive achievements of any fan community for any game".<ref name=pcgameruk2x>{{cite magazine | last=Gillen | first=Kieron | author-link=Kieron Gillen | title=Five Perfect Crimes | magazine=[[PC Gamer UK]] | issue=151 | date=August 2005 | page=106 }}</ref>
